item.title: Pope will meet with survivors of clergy abuse during upcoming trip to Latin America, Vatican says
item.description:
Pope will meet with survivors of clergy abuse during upcoming trip to Latin America, Vatican says
The Vatican says Pope Leo XIV will meet with survivors of clergy sexual abuse during his upcoming trip to Latin AmericaByThe Associated PressOctober 27, 2026, 12:05 PM
ROME -- ROME (AP) — Pope Leo XIV will meet with survivors of clergy sexual abuse during his upcoming trip to Latin America, which will take the American pope to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, the Vatican said Tuesday.
The Vatican statement didn’t say when the encounters would take place or where, but said “several meetings are planned,” suggesting more than one encounter. The Nov. 6-17 trip is going ahead as planned despite Leo's Oct. 13 lung cancer surgery which had put the trip in question.
Continuing the practice of his two recent predecessors, Leo met with abuse survivors in June in Spain and most recently in France. Ahead of the French trip, the Vatican confirmed the meeting ahead of time rather than after it took place, as had been the previous practice.
“These meetings reflect the pope’s desire to express his solidarity with those who have suffered and continue to suffer as a result of this violence, to work with them to build paths to healing that are accessible to anyone in need, and to ensure that the church is a safe and spiritually healthy place that lives out and communicates the Gospel,” according to a Vatican statement Tuesday.
Leo spent two decades as a missionary priest in Peru, and he saw first-hand the effects of abuse on victims. He was the designated bishop in the Peruvian bishops conference to hear from victims of an influential but abusive movement, the Sodalitium Christianae Vitae.

item.title: Serbia’s victorious student movement faces tough challenges as it prepares to take power
item.description:
Serbia’s victorious student movement faces tough challenges as it prepares to take power
Serbia’s youth movement pulled out a stunning election victory at the weekend against the country’s long-time strongman ruler Aleksandar VucicByJOVANA GEC Associated PressOctober 27, 2026, 11:27 AM
BELGRADE, Serbia -- Serbia's youth movement pulled out a stunning election victory against the country's long-time strongman ruler Aleksandar Vucic. But turning its promises of sweeping democratic reforms into reality could prove far more difficult.
The leaderless and diverse movement with few candidates with experience in politics has promised to root out corruption, free the media and guarantee the rule of law it says have been ravaged during Vucic's 14 years in power.
Though armed with a strong mandate for change stemming from a convincing election victory, a new government will still encounter a myriad of hurdles along the way. Expectations are running high and so is impatience after public discontent built over years.
Here is a look at the challenges that lie ahead:
Though Vucic conceded defeat just an hour and a half after polls closed on Sunday, it's likely to take weeks before a new government is formed.
Serbia's election laws provide for a period of appeals and potential reruns at individual polling stations before final election results are announced and a new Parliament is inaugurated. Any meaningful policy changes can only take place after a new government takes office.
Serbia’s state election commission so far has released only preliminary and incomplete results of the vote on Sunday, but they are unlikely to change much — the Students’ List is set to have a comfortable majority of 140 seats in the 250-member Parliament while Vucic’s SNS party will have 104.

item.title: A tornado rips through a construction site in Turkey, killing 4 workers
item.description:
A tornado rips through a construction site in Turkey, killing 4 workers
A tornado has hit a construction site in Antalya, Turkey, killing four workers and injuring anotherByThe Associated PressOctober 27, 2026, 7:13 AM
ANTALYA, Turkey -- A tornado hit a construction site in the Mediterranean coastal province of Antalya early on Tuesday, destroying a container housing workers and killing four of them, an official said.
A fifth worker, who was staying inside another container, was injured in the powerful storm that struck the building site in Antalya’s Kepez district, Gov. Hulusi Sahin told reporters.
Three of the workers who were killed were Syrian nationals, Sahin said. There was no immediate information on the condition of the injured worker.
The tornado, which came shortly after the country’s weather agency warned of heavy rains, also knocked down a crane at the site, Sahin said.

item.title: Cyclone Arnab hits India's Andhra Pradesh state as tens of thousands evacuate
item.description:
Cyclone Arnab hits India's Andhra Pradesh state as tens of thousands evacuate
Officials say Cyclone Arnab crossed India’s Andhra Pradesh coast early Wednesday, a day after tens of thousands of people were forced to evacuate from vulnerable coastal areas in the eastern stateByOMER FAROOQ Associated PressOctober 27, 2026, 11:58 PM
Share
HYDERABAD, India -- Cyclone Arnab crossed India 's Andhra Pradesh coast in the early hours of Wednesday, officials said, a day after tens of thousands of people were evacuated from vulnerable coastal areas in the eastern state.
Prakhar Jain, head of the state’s disaster management authority, said the cyclone had weakened slightly before landfall but brought heavy to very heavy rainfall to several coastal districts, triggering widespread disruption in affected areas.
State disaster management officials said late Wednesday morning that wind speeds were up to 135 kph (84 mph).
Officials said the cyclone was expected to weaken further as it moved inland, with wind speeds likely to ease later in the day.
There were no immediate reports of casualties, but some damage was observed.
The India Meteorological Department said the landfall process was complete and heavy rainfall as well as strong winds would continue under the cyclone's influence in coastal areas of Andhra Pradesh and parts of southern Odisha state.
Cyclone Arnab weakened to a "severe" cyclonic storm Wednesday, IMD said in an update.

item.title: Tanzania’s jailed opposition leader ends hunger strike after meeting with his brother
item.description:
Tanzania’s jailed opposition leader ends hunger strike after meeting with his brother
Tanzania’s jailed opposition leader Tundu Lissu has ended a brief hunger strike after prison authorities allowed him to meet privately with his younger brotherByKHALED KAZZIHA Associated PressOctober 27, 2026, 10:59 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
NAIROBI, Kenya -- Tanzania’s jailed opposition leader Tundu Lissu ended a brief hunger strike Tuesday after prison authorities allowed him to meet privately with his younger brother, his lead lawyer said.
Lissu, who survived being shot 16 times in a 2017 assassination attempt and has spent periods in exile citing threats to his life, leads Tanzania’s main opposition party, Chadema.
He faces a treason charge carrying a possible death sentence and has been detained for more than 18 months, with a final judgment scheduled for Nov. 6.
His lead lawyer, Rugemeleza Nshala, told The Associated Press by telephone that Lissu had planned to begin the strike Monday to protest restrictions on court-ordered confidential legal consultations. He postponed it after prison authorities promised private access.
When those consultations failed to take place Monday, Lissu began refusing food Tuesday morning, Nshala said.
“Lissu did not take his tea, breakfast or lunch,” Nshala said. He ended the strike after lunchtime following the private meeting with his brother.
Prison authorities and the government had issued no public statements on the hunger strike.
Nshala said Saturday that prison authorities had, on some occasions, barred access to Lissu altogether. He expressed concern about the health implications of a hunger strike because Lissu relies on medication.
Lissu was arrested April 9, 2025, after addressing a rally calling for electoral reforms ahead of that year’s general election and was charged with treason the following day.

item.title: Attacks kill at least 60 Orthodox Christians in Ethiopia, church says
item.description:
Attacks kill at least 60 Orthodox Christians in Ethiopia, church says
The Ethiopian Orthodox Church reports that two attacks in Oromia have killed at least 60 Orthodox ChristiansByKHALED KAZZIHA Associated PressOctober 27, 2026, 8:37 AM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
NAIROBI, Kenya -- Two attacks in Ethiopia’s Oromia region killed at least 60 Orthodox Christians, the country’s Orthodox Church said, urging authorities to protect civilians and bring those responsible to justice.
The Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church’s Holy Synod said Monday that 14 people were killed in Merti district on Oct. 20 and a further 46 in Shirka district on Saturday. Both districts are in Oromia’s Arsi Zone.
More than 20 people were seriously wounded and 20 homes were burned down, the church said, describing the killings as “brutal and merciless massacres.”
A Christian resident of a nearby town said he traveled to Tereta Chole, the village in Shirka district where Saturday's attack took place, to attend funerals Saturday and help transport the wounded. “We counted the injured people who were loaded onto the Isuzu truck,” he said.
A priest based in the same nearby town said he saw wounded people arriving at the hospital near his home. Some patients were later referred to other hospitals, he said. Both men spoke to The Associated Press by telephone on condition of anonymity because they feared for their safety.
Oromia regional government spokesperson Hailu Adugna blamed the Oromo Liberation Army, or OLA, for the attacks. He accused the rebels and their allies of trying to provoke ethnic and religious conflict to divert attention from military losses in northern Ethiopia. He presented no evidence in the statement to support the accusations.
Adugna expressed sorrow over the deaths and destruction and said that regional authorities had begun taking action against those responsible. He pledged assistance to people wounded or displaced.
The OLA couldn't be reached for comment. ...

item.title: Court orders closure of one of Egypt's last independent media outlets, detains and fines editor
item.description:
Court orders closure of one of Egypt's last independent media outlets, detains and fines editor
A court has ordered the closure of one of Egypt’s last independent news outlets, Mada Masr, after convicting its editor-in-chief on charges of operating a website without a licenseByThe Associated PressOctober 27, 2026, 12:53 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
An Egyptian court ordered the closure of one of Egypt’s last independent news outlets Tuesday after convicting its editor-in-chief of operating a website without a license in a major blow to the country's shrinking press freedom.
The publication, Mada Masr, said its editor-in-chief and founder, Lina Attalah, was ordered to pay a fine equivalent to about $53,400. After the verdict, the judge ordered Attalah detained until the fine is paid.
Mada Masr was one of the few remaining news outlets in Egypt known for investigating corruption, the expanding role of the country's powerful military, and human rights violations in a country where newspapers and television stations are closely controlled by authorities. Ahead of Tuesday’s hearing, Human Rights Watch called the prosecution of Attalah an escalation of an “outrageous attack on independent media.”
Attalah’s lead lawyer, Hassan el-Azhary, said Mada Masr planned to appeal the closure order.
“Today’s decision represents a crushing blow to press freedom in Egypt and marks a dark day for independent journalism in the country," Amnesty International said in a statement. By imposing a large fine, ordering the closure of Mada Masr and the seizure of its property, while ”detaining Lina Attalah until payment is made, the Egyptian authorities are sending a clear and ruthless message: critical, independent reporting will not be tolerated."
Although the fine was paid a few hours after the verdict, Attalah’s whereabouts remain unknown, according to a statement by Mada Masr on social media.

item.title: Top Vatican official says pope's cancer diagnosis a 'game-changer' for the papacy
item.description:
Top Vatican official says pope's cancer diagnosis a 'game-changer' for the papacy
A top Vatican official says that Pope Leo XIV's lung cancer diagnosis is “a bit of a gamechanger” for the VaticanByNICOLE WINFIELD Associated PressOctober 27, 2026, 3:14 PM
ShareFollow ABC News on Google
ROME -- Even though Pope Leo XIV is recovering well from lung cancer surgery and is going ahead with a big trip to Latin America next week, the diagnosis is “a bit of a game-changer” for the Vatican and Leo’s still-young papacy, a top Vatican official said Tuesday.
Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher, the Holy See’s foreign minister, said there had been a temptation to think that Leo was a “Superman, a Superpope” after he was elected in 2025 and “hit the ground running” following the drawn-out illness and death of Pope Francis.
“The fact that he has fallen ill with, in many ways, one of the most common illnesses of our age means that he is a poor mortal like the rest of us. And I think that that is going to change how we see him and possibly how he sees himself as well,” Gallagher told reporters at the Italian foreign press association.
“Even if the operation has gone well, and everybody (says) there are grounds for considerable optimism, I think it is a bit of a game-changer at the same time,” Gallagher said.
Leo, 71, had the lower lobe of his right lung removed Oct. 13 after doctors found a tumor, later diagnosed as adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. Subsequent tests indicated no further treatment is necessary, and Leo has been slowly resuming his daily activities.
The Vatican this week confirmed Leo would go ahead with his planned Nov. 6-17 trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru, without any changes to the program. The published trip itinerary is challenging even for a healthy pope, with a dozen flights and two helicopter rides covering 31,000 kilometers (19,000 miles), the longest of Leo’s pontificate.

item.title: German court rejects bid to end Ukrainian ex-officer's trial over Nord Stream pipeline blasts
item.description:
German court rejects bid to end Ukrainian ex-officer's trial over Nord Stream pipeline blasts
A German court has rejected a defense request to end the trial of a former Ukrainian army officer who is accused of damaging the Nord Stream gas pipelines built to carry Russian gas to Western Europe in blasts four years agoByThe Associated PressOctober 27, 2026, 7:15 AM
HAMBURG, Germany -- A German court on Tuesday rejected a defense request to end the trial of a former Ukrainian army officer who is accused of damaging the Nord Stream gas pipelines built to carry Russian gas to western Europe in blasts four years ago.
Serhii Kuznietsov, 50, went on trial at the Hamburg state court on Oct. 14, charged with causing an explosion, damaging property, disrupting public service and being an “accomplice to war crimes” by attacking civilian infrastructure.
He is alleged to have been the ringleader of the attack on the Nord Stream gas pipelines, considered one of Europe’s biggest acts of sabotage since World War II.
His lawyers swiftly filed a motion to dismiss the charges. They argued that Kuznietsov was still an active duty soldier and as such was obligated by Ukrainian law not to speak for reasons of secrecy linked to national security, and that under German law anyone who can't speak out can't be convicted.
The court dismissed the motion on the trial's second day of hearings on Tuesday, German news agency dpa reported. It said that the defendant's defense wasn't limited under German law, and that freedom to testify in Germany isn't limited by a foreign country's conditions of service.

item.title: Environmentalists celebrate Lula's reelection in Brazil
item.description:
Environmentalists celebrate Lula's reelection in Brazil
Environmentalists, Indigenous groups and climate scientists are relieved after President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's reelection in BrazilByGABRIELA SÁ PESSOA Associated PressOctober 27, 2026, 12:55 AM
MANAUS, Brazil -- Environmentalists, Indigenous groups and climate scientists are celebrating the reelection in Brazil of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, which brings the prospect of a continued focus on stopping the illegal cutting of the Amazon, the largest rainforest in the world.
But supporters also warned that a Congress increasingly dominated by the far right and the agribusiness caucus could undermine those efforts to protect the forest and combat climate change.
Lula defeated Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, son of far-right former President Jair Bolsonaro, in Sunday’s runoff with 51.78% of the vote to 48.21%. After trailing in the first round, Lula staged a comeback to win by 4.4 million votes.
“The Amazon can breathe a sigh of relief!” said David Lapola, a Brazilian scientist and lead author of a chapter on so-called tipping points in an upcoming United Nations climate report. Scientists debate the threshold beyond which the dense, humid Amazon rainforest could shift to a drier ecosystem, with irreversible consequences for biodiversity and the climate. The forest absorbs vast amounts of carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas that drives global warming. About 60% of the Amazon lies in Brazil.
Lula’s victory reflected shifts in voter support and higher turnout nationwide. In the Amazon, Indigenous communities and advocacy groups mobilized voters and, aided by court rulings last week, helped secure government transportation for those living in remote areas.
